Bought it cause I'm into Orwell and dystopian stories and such. Was very disappointed. You click on a page and either look for the clickable blue text or waste your time and read it and get immersed like I did. To put it simply, boring. But I stuck with it and gave it a shot. What really grinds my gears is the yellow text. It is supposed to be "contradictory" statements, but is anything but.

For example, the first woman you investigate has two posts that "contradict" each other where in one post she calls another woman her best friend and in the other she gets mad at said woman. THAT. IS. NOT. CONTRADICTORY. IF ANYTHING, getting frustrated and having strained relationships with friends is extremely common. But you can only pick one making the story that she either "hates the woman" or "is her best friend" instead of the simple truth that she is her best friend AND they get into fights as can be explained later by the woman being off of her meds.

If you're someone who doesn't like this type of game, you won't enjoy it so don't buy it. If you do enjoy this type of game, you'll likely be disappointed like I was and won't enjoy it, so don't buy it. Not worth even at a sale.

If the game doesn't want you clicking on a certain item, it just sends you through a series of loops of graphics, which can also be confusing at the start of the game when you're trying to figure out what matters and what will change throughout the 'day' in the investigation. The interface, while accurate, really does remind you of your work computer. That's... not a compliment.

Some of the interesting questions this game briefly poses never get answered - including fleshing out details of certain characters you have compromising information on. In reality, you're not engaging with 90% of the text it tries to force-feed you. You're just searching for highlighted blurbs to obediently click and pass to the next marker. It's disappointing because it could have been so much more.

There’s something oddly calming about these kinds of games. No button-mashing, no reflex tests, no “oops I fell off the roof again” moments. Just me, a cup of coffee, a comfy chair, and the soft hum of moral ambiguity.

Orwell lets you dig, decide, and doubt. It’s like being a digital detective with a slight caffeine addiction and an increasing concern for how twisted “logic” can get when filtered through surveillance systems and personal bias.
You’ll click around, feel clever, feel conflicted – and occasionally yell at the screen because "wait, that’s not what I meant!"

But do I regret anything?
Absolutely not. That’s the beauty of it: different choices, different outcomes, different little identity crises.

Highly recommend if you enjoy quiet intensity, ethical dilemmas, and feeling both powerful and powerless at the same time.

I'm surprised how lukewarm a lot of the reviews of this game are - I thought it was phenomenal! I guess it's because the game is mostly reading?

The government has created a piece of software designed to spy on anyone and everyone with the aim of catching criminals and terrorists. You are recruited as an investigator tasked with using it to create profiles of suspicious individuals, going through their emails, phones, desktops, etc... aiming to find anything incriminating.

Although it might seem obvious that an all-powerful piece of spying software may be somewhat unethical, Orwell does a great job at making you [i]experience[/i] it. When you're listening in on a suspect's phone call and rather than anything incriminating you just hear an argument between a couple going through a hard time in their relationship, you feel kinda gross. When you label somebody as angry and hateful based on a blog post they wrote years ago, which you later found out they regret, you get a pit in your stomach realising that the profile you made of them could have a big negative impact on this person's life in the future.

Saying that, the game doesn't feel preachy. You [i]are[/i] able to use the software to hunt down and reveal criminals who may have otherwise gone scot-free, and the game makes it clear that increased surveillance [i]is[/i] leading to dramatic reductions in crime. So does that make the gross invasion of privacy ultimately justified?? I really enjoyed how conflicted I felt up to the very end and how much it made me think.

This is a game where your choices really do matter, different people may live, die, or be arrested in your playthrough based on the choices that you make. I actually replayed the final chapter a second time because I wasn't satisfied with my ending, and managed to unlock a lot of extra information I didn't get the first time. 

I was super gripped the whole way through and am excited to play the sequel now!

I appreciated this since I didn't really want to skip through dialogue for several hours just to discover what was actually going on.

The theme is strong but surprisingly not preachy. You have to imagine, based on the name and the premise, that the writers are pretty pro-privacy but the game never feels like it's going out of its way to punish you if you play in a different way. The writing is strong enough that the logical conclusion of your actions will force you to consider your morality and I consider that to be a major strength of the game's story.

Orwell won't likely blow your mind and it doesn't quite go hard enough into the free form investigation that I personally craved but it's a fun 5 hours that will give you some fun puzzles to solve and some moral issues to consider.

I first found this game after watching an Australian streamer play a little of it after PAX AUS. I loved the concept and what I saw, but nothing prepared me for how much I actually enjoyed it when playing it.

The game is simple in its mechanics, working a little like a computer screen. It is text-based with pictures and images, a computer style, and really cool music that makes up for no voices. It doesn't need any. The ambience makes you feel everything as you read. And it is especially good for a stream game - lots of talking for you as you read, great music, and amazing twists and turns.

And that is what this game is - a story game where choices make differences to how the story plays out, and there are lots of twists/big moments that keep you invested. I won't spoil the game or story for you, but if you enjoy story games, or dystopian societies, or stories with meanings and choices in them, then this is for you!

Finished the game in roughly 3.5 hours. It has good potential, a semi-interesting story line, and the game mechanics are easy to pick up and understand. However, I can't say I really recommend this game. I never felt a connection with the characters that I have gotten from other games of this style such as Cyber Manhunt (1 and 2) (which I highly recommend if you liked this game or were unsatisfied and want something more in-depth). Like I said earlier, the game mechanics and very easy, everything is already highlighted for you. However, this makes the game a little boring in my opinion and takes the player away from wanting to actually read what is going on. 

My biggest issue with the game though is the "conflicting data" portion. There is never really any evidence to allow the player to make an informed decision and if there was, there is not enough incentive to read the rest of the text to figure it out. There are some instances where one datachunk seems more trustworthy than another (SPOILER) such as when choosing between whether the founder of "Thought" is truly gay or not (I can't believe I just typed that). 

If you like dystopian themes and point-and-click style games, this could be a great fit for you. However, as someone who values the difficulty of the game, especially when it comes to "hacker" or "big-brother" style games, and player engagement, it just isn't for me.

"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" is an outstanding game that had me hooked from start to finish. The developers have masterfully crafted a gripping and unsettling story that tackles contemporary issues such as surveillance, privacy, and ethics.

The gameplay mechanics are unique and innovative. As a player, you take on the role of an investigator who sifts through data and analyzes information to uncover threats to national security. Throughout the game, you are faced with moral decisions that significantly impact the storyline. These choices are often challenging and thought-provoking, making the game a deeply engaging experience.

The atmosphere of the game is excellently executed. The visual design and soundtrack contribute to creating a dense and suspenseful mood. What is particularly impressive is how realistic and believable the world of "Orwell" feels. You truly feel like a part of this dystopian society.

Another highlight is the storytelling. The narrative is thrilling and full of twists that constantly surprise you. The characters are well-developed, and their fates are compelling. You quickly form an emotional connection with the characters and find yourself rooting for them.

Overall, "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" is a masterpiece that not only entertains but also makes you think. It is a game that stays with you long after you have finished playing. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for an intelligent and captivating game.
